references.title: Design for Ionizing Radiation Protection (NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-020)
references.publisher: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer
references.fact: An astronaut's career radiation dose must stay under 600 mSv, and one solar particle event under 250 mSv. Aluminium and polyethylene shielding cut solar-storm dose by about half. A storm shelter adds about 10 cm of water, made by moving water containers. On the Moon's surface the background dose is about 0.5 mSv a day.

references.title: Earth's Moon: Facts
references.fact: One side of the Moon gets about two weeks of sunlight, then about two weeks of darkness. The surface reaches about 127 °C in full Sun and about −173 °C in the dark. Ice is found in permanently shadowed craters at the poles.

references.title: A Deployable 40 kWe Lunar Fission Surface Power Concept (NTRS 20220004670)
references.fact: NASA studied a 40 kilowatt fission reactor for the Moon, because future crews, science and resource mining need continuous power, day and night. It would stand at least 1 km from the base.

references.title: NASA Fuel Cell Tests Pave Way for Energy Storage on Moon
references.fact: A regenerative fuel cell works like a rechargeable battery: it joins hydrogen and oxygen into water to make electricity, and splits the water again to recharge. It could carry a base through the cold, dark, nearly two-week lunar night and weigh less than batteries storing the same energy.

references.title: Carbon Dioxide (NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-004)
references.publisher: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer
references.fact: In a study of 49 space station astronauts, 19 reported headaches, and headaches went with higher carbon dioxide levels. NASA's standard keeps cabin CO2 below 3 mmHg.

references.title: Growing Plants in Space
references.fact: Veggie, the space station's garden, grows plants under red and blue LED lights, with water and fertilizer in small pillows. Fresh food helps prevent vitamin shortages on long missions and makes the crew feel better.

references.title: Toolkit for educators and youth: Food production on the Moon and in remote areas
references.fact: The Canadian Space Agency explains how growing food in space connects to astronauts' health and nutrition, and how the same ideas can help remote communities on Earth.

references.title: Overview: In-Situ Resource Utilization
references.fact: Water ice is buried under the Moon's soil in some places; the LCROSS impact found that nearly five percent of the soil it hit was water. NASA plans to turn that ice into drinking water and oxygen.

references.title: NASA's Artemis Base Camp on the Moon Will Need Light, Water, Elevation
references.fact: Near the south pole, high ridges and crater rims get long periods of sunlight for power, while crater floors stay dark and may hold frozen water for life support. Planners trade sunlight against distance to the ice.

references.title: To Protect Artemis II Astronauts, NASA Experts Keep Eyes on Sun
references.fact: NASA and NOAA watch the Sun around the clock during crewed flights. If radiation rises past a threshold, the crew is told to shelter: they move stowed gear against the walls, because mass absorbs the particles.

references.title: Solar Storms and Flares
references.fact: Flares are ranked C, M and X. Each letter is about ten times stronger than the one before, so an X flare is 100 times stronger than a C flare. Fast particles from solar eruptions are a radiation risk to astronauts.

references.title: Evidence Report: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload
references.fact: Space station astronauts sleep less in space than on the ground. NASA counts 10-hour work days on more than 3 days a week as a critical overload, because tired crews make more mistakes.

references.title: Evidence Report: Risk of Inadequate Food System
references.fact: Space station crews get about 1.8 kg of food plus packaging per person per day, and all of it has to be launched.

references.title: Money Mass-ematics
references.fact: Every kilogram launched adds cost and energy, so mission planners count every kilogram they pack.

references.title: Managing NASA's International Space Station Logistics and Maintenance Program (NTRS 20100033370)
references.fact: The space station is kept running by swapping broken units for spare ones carried on board, because help from Earth takes a long time to arrive.

references.title: Protecting Crew and Surface Systems with a Long-Duration Lunar Safe Haven (NTRS 20210022066)
references.fact: Moon soil (regolith) piled 3 to 7 m thick over a base is good radiation shielding, and machines could dig and pile it.

references.title: LunaNet
references.fact: Relay satellites will keep crews at the lunar south pole in touch with Earth, even where Earth can't be seen in the sky.

references.title: Spacewalk Spacesuit Basics
references.fact: A spacesuit's backpack holds the oxygen the astronaut breathes and removes the carbon dioxide they breathe out. A walk outside lasts several hours and uses up these supplies.

references.title: Extraterrestrial Surface Transport Vehicles: Rovers (NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-023)
references.publisher: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer
references.fact: The Apollo rover's battery could have driven 92 km, but crews never went further than 7.6 km: the 'walkback limit', the furthest they could walk home if it broke.

references.title: DONKI: Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information
references.fact: NASA's record of real solar flares, coronal mass ejections, solar energetic particle events and geomagnetic storms. The game's solar storms are real events from it.

references.title: NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR)
references.fact: NASA's public archive of space biology and astronaut health research. The game links a few of its real studies to the crew's health and the greenhouse.

references.title: Assessment of the State of Communication Delay Research in Preparation for Missions Beyond Low Earth Orbit (NASA/TM–20250003885)
references.fact: Lunar missions may see one-way communication delays of 3 to 14 seconds. NASA expects about 5.6 seconds for voice from Earth on Artemis (Orion), against 1.3 seconds for Apollo telemetry.
